channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Aviation
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] NTSB ties a fatal New Mexico air-ambulance crash to GPS jamming from an authorised military exercise — not a cyberattack
item.description: In May 2026, a Hawker air ambulance crashed near Ruidoso, New Mexico, killing all four people aboard. NTSB investigators have since tied the loss of GPS signal aboard the aircraft to an authorised electronic-warfare training exercise under way at the nearby White Sands Missile Range. This is a radio-frequency interference and safety-of-navigation event, not a cyberattack: no network was breached, no device was hacked, and no malicious actor was involved. The exercise itself was lawful military activity, but the interference it produced reportedly reached beyond the intended test area and degraded satellite navigation for at least this aircraft during a time-critical medevac flight. Pilots and air traffic controllers in the region have filed GPS-interference reports for roughly a decade, according to follow-up coverage, without that pattern translating into changed procedures before this crash. Because the flight was an air-ambulance mission, the loss of reliable position data compounded an already safety-sensitive, low-margin operation. Broader follow-up reporting examines expanding military jamming exercises and unauthorised drone activity as a growing navigation-safety risk for civil aviation generally, not only around this one range. This item sits on a cyber threat dashboard because GNSS integrity underpins the same navigation and surveillance infrastructure that a cyberattack could also degrade, and a signal-loss event with this consequence is an operational and safety failure regardless of its cause. Four people died in this incident, and it should be read on its own terms rather than folded into cyber-incident statistics. - NTSB investigation; follow-up reporting — via WWNO/NPR - Reported 13 Aug 2026 (crash May 2026)

item.title: [High] CISA and the FBI refresh the Medusa advisory past 500 critical-infrastructure victims — and flag exploits used before disclosure
item.description: CISA and the FBI updated their #StopRansomware advisory on Medusa on 18 Aug 2026. The cumulative victim count passed 500 critical-infrastructure organisations as of April 2026, up from roughly 300 in the March 2025 version — about 200 new victims in a year. Named sectors are healthcare, critical manufacturing, the defense industrial base, government facilities, IT and financial services; aviation is not among them, and the advisory alleges no control-system involvement. Impact is enterprise-IT encryption plus data theft. The detail worth carrying into an airport or airline programme is timing: the agencies report Medusa weaponises newly disclosed vulnerabilities within about 24 hours, and has been observed using exploits up to a week before public disclosure, buying capability rather than developing it. That compresses the exposure window to something well short of the change-control cycle most terminal facilities and airline IT estates actually run on. - CISA/FBI #StopRansomware advisory AA25-071A (updated) - Updated 18 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] CISA’s Gunra ransomware advisory lands as Dragos counts six aviation incidents in a rising industrial wave
item.description: CISA and international partners issued a joint #StopRansomware advisory on Gunra, a Conti-derived ransomware-as-a-service operation using double extortion against government and critical-infrastructure targets, typically gaining initial access through unpatched internet-facing VPN gateways and exposed RDP, including known Fortinet flaws. It arrives alongside Dragos’s Q2 2026 finding of 1,140 industrial ransomware incidents overall, up 12% quarter on quarter, of which 95 hit transportation and logistics — 8 maritime, 6 aviation, 3 rail. Dragos found no case this quarter of ransomware operators directly manipulating an industrial control system; disruption came through IT and virtualisation layers instead. For an airport or airline, that IT layer typically carries stand and gate allocation, baggage reconciliation, crew rostering and flight-information displays — none individually safety-critical, all required for a normal operating day. Gunra’s extortion notes cite a five-to-seven-day payment deadline. - CISA/FBI joint advisory AA26-222A; Dragos Q2 2026 industrial ransomware analysis - Advisories published 10 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Two critical, unauthenticated flaws in Johnson Controls C-CURE 9000 and victor could hand over an airport’s access-control system
item.description: Johnson Controls’ updated advisory (Update A, 11 Aug) covers three vulnerabilities in the C-CURE 9000 access-control platform and the victor video management system: CVE-2026-21655 and CVE-2026-21653, two critical unauthenticated deserialization flaws with CVSS scores up to 9.6, plus a high-severity issue tracked as CVE-2026-34496. A network-adjacent attacker could exploit the deserialization bugs to execute arbitrary code and take control of the physical access-control system without any credentials. C-CURE 9000 and victor are widely deployed for badge access, door control and CCTV integration in airport terminals, airside gates and secured operational areas, which makes this one of the more consequential advisories this window for aviation specifically, even though no exploitation has been reported. - Johnson Controls advisory; CISA ICSA-26-204-01 - Update A published 11 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] A CVSS 9.1 command-injection flaw in Siemens Siveillance Video sits on the platform that runs terminal and apron CCTV
item.description: CISA advisory ICSA-26-225-09 covers CVE-2026-3014, an OS command injection flaw scored CVSS 9.1 in the Management Server API of Siemens Siveillance Video. Any user holding edit permissions on the Management Server can run arbitrary commands in the context of the Management Server Service. Hotfixes are available for V2023R3 below v23.3.27, V2024R1 below v24.1.16 and V2025 below v25.1.15. Siveillance is a video management system deployed for terminal, apron, perimeter and access-point surveillance, which makes the consequence two-sided: code execution on a server that usually sits trusted inside the security network, and influence over what the operations or security control centre is looking at. No exploitation has been reported, and the flaw needs an existing privileged account rather than anonymous network access. - CISA ICSA-26-225-09; Siemens ProductCERT - Published 13 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Johnson Controls Metasys flaw lets a low-privilege user reach an administrator’s session — and versions 12 and 13 are end of support
item.description: CISA advisory ICSA-26-225-14 covers CVE-2026-34491, a persistent cross-site scripting flaw scored CVSS 8.0 in Johnson Controls Metasys. A low-privilege Metasys user can plant a payload through a crafted URL that then executes in an administrator’s browser, inheriting that administrator’s reach over the building management system. Metasys 12 and 13 are affected in all versions, 14 below 14.1.5 and 15 below 15.0.1; version 15.0 was patched on 25 Mar 2026 and 16.0 ships with the fix. The sting is in the lifecycle: 12 and 13 are end of support, so for those estates the remedy is an upgrade project rather than a patch. Metasys is among the most widely deployed building management platforms in airport terminals, governing HVAC, lighting and plant that a terminal’s operating day depends on. No exploitation has been reported. - CISA ICSA-26-225-14; Johnson Controls advisory - Published 13 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Two of CISA’s four KEV additions on 18 August land squarely on the remote-access and virtualisation layers airports run on
item.description: CISA added four vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 18 Aug 2026, all carrying a 21 Aug federal remediation deadline. Two matter directly for aviation infrastructure. CVE-2026-33824 is a double-free flaw in the Microsoft Windows IKE Extensions service (IKEEXT) leading to remote code execution — IKE and IPsec are what terminate airline tenant links, site-to-site connections to remote facilities and vendor remote support into ground systems. CVE-2026-59310 is a Broadcom VMware vCenter path-traversal flaw leading to code execution, already under mass exploitation before the listing formalised it; airport and airline supervisory workloads, from flight-information displays to building-management front ends and historians, increasingly run as guests on that estate. The other two additions are Microsoft SharePoint (CVE-2026-55040) and Apple macOS Screen Sharing (CVE-2026-65400). A three-day deadline is itself a statement about exploitation scale. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue - Added 18 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] CISA’s 15-advisory day includes a Siemens Desigo flaw that can freeze an airport building controller
item.description: CISA published 15 ICS advisories in a single day on 13 Aug 2026, spanning AVEVA, Hitachi Energy, ANDRITZ, Siemens and Johnson Controls. Among them, CVE-2026-59693 (CVSS 4.3) affects Siemens Desigo DXR2 and PXC3/4/5/7 building controllers: a malformed BACnet packet can stop the controller responding until it is manually reset. Desigo is a building-management platform used in HVAC, lighting and life-safety integration, including at airports, where a frozen controller during a terminal operating day is a facilities incident even without any data compromised. Firmware updates are available. None of the advisories in this 15-advisory batch have been reported as exploited. - Siemens ProductCERT; CISA ICS advisories, 13 Aug 2026 batch - Published 13 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] Johnson Controls fixes a hardcoded key and a path-traversal flaw in its Airwall secure remote-access product
item.description: Johnson Controls patched two vulnerabilities in Airwall, its OT secure remote-access product: CVE-2026-64887, a hardcoded cryptographic key (CVSS 6.8), and CVE-2026-34492, a path-traversal flaw allowing arbitrary file read (CVSS 6.4). Both are fixed in version 4.1.0. CISA rates neither remotely exploitable at low attack complexity, which limits urgency, but Airwall’s role is notable: it is a secure-remote-access product airports and airlines may already use specifically to reduce the kind of internet-exposed control access seen in the water-sector PLC campaign, so a flaw in the access broker itself is worth tracking even at moderate severity. - CISA ICSA-26-225-03; Johnson Controls advisory - Published 13 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] USENIX researchers show that ~60 seconds of physical access to a Boeing 737 maintenance port can alter flight data
item.description: Academic researchers from UC San Diego and Oberlin, presenting at USENIX Security 2026, built a sub-$100, coin-sized ESP32 device that, inserted through an unlocked maintenance port, can intercept and override ARINC 429 traffic between the flight management computer and the display unit on a Boeing 737. Once connected, the device can alter flight plans, autopilot settings or weight-and-balance data, and the researchers say roughly 60 seconds of unsupervised physical access is enough to install it. Boeing states that the aircraft’s layered design and existing operational protections mitigate the risk; the researchers disagree that the issue is fully resolved. This is a proof of concept demonstrated in a research setting, not an observed exploitation, and it requires physical access to an unlocked port rather than any remote or network entry — which makes it a ramp, turnaround and MRO access-control question as much as an avionics one. - USENIX Security 2026 research (UC San Diego, Oberlin) - Presented Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] Six flaws in CISA’s own Malcolm OT monitoring suite are a reminder that the sensor is part of the attack surface
item.description: CISA advisory ICSA-26-230-01 discloses six vulnerabilities in Malcolm, CISA’s own open-source OT network traffic analysis suite. The most serious, CVE-2026-55676 (CVSS 8.8), is an unrestricted file upload leading to arbitrary code execution; the others cover path traversal during archive extraction (CVE-2026-63177, 7.1), a role-based access-control bypass via unnormalised URI paths (CVE-2026-63134), a percent-encoding authorization bypass (CVE-2026-19670) and two further issues, alongside resource-exhaustion denial of service. Fixes land in Malcolm 26.07.0 and 26.08.0 depending on the CVE. No exploitation has been reported. It earns a place on an aviation page because of where Malcolm sits: typically inside the OT network on a SPAN or TAP feed, with visibility of baggage, building-management and airfield traffic. A monitoring platform in that position is an unusually well-placed foothold if it is compromised, and it is often the one system nobody has threat-modelled because it is the security tool. - CISA ICSA-26-230-01 - Published 18 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] GAO: TSA is still working from a 2018 cybersecurity roadmap, and FAA has fully implemented three of seven strategy objectives
item.description: GAO’s aviation cybersecurity review, GAO-26-107693, found that TSA has not clearly defined cybersecurity roles and responsibilities for the aviation sector and is still operating against a Cybersecurity Roadmap issued in 2018 that no longer aligns with current DHS strategy. On the FAA side, GAO found the agency has not fully reported its cybersecurity spending to OMB, and that its Zero Trust Implementation Plan only partially aligns with recognised NIST practice; of the seven objectives in FAA’s own Cybersecurity Strategy, three had been fully implemented. GAO issued five recommendations and the departments accepted them. Published in July, it remains the current federal assessment, and in a window with no aviation incident it is the most substantive aviation-specific item on this page. The practical read for an operator is that federal role clarity is still being built, so do not assume a coordinating body already owns a gap at your airport. - GAO-26-107693, Aviation Cybersecurity - Published 16 Jul 2026; five recommendations accepted

item.title: [Low] FAA issues a $74.3M initial task order to begin replacing the network behind air traffic control
item.description: The FAA awarded AT&T a $74.3 million initial task order on 14 Aug 2026 under what is anticipated to become a multibillion-dollar, 15-year programme to modernise the telecommunications network underpinning air traffic control. This is a procurement milestone, not a security event: nothing in it indicates a compromise, a vulnerability or an attack. It sits on this page because the infrastructure being replaced is the aging ATC networking that GAO and others have repeatedly flagged in resilience assessments, and because a multi-year national network transition is itself a security programme. Cutover windows, parallel running of legacy and new circuits, and a much larger population of contractor hands on operationally critical links all create risk that has to be managed deliberately. How cybersecurity requirements are written into the individual task orders will matter more over the programme’s life than the headline contract value. - FAA contract award reporting — via Nextgov/FCW - Awarded 14 Aug 2026
